sentence_as_it_stands: Its neuropathic-pain evidence is thin and almost entirely uncontrolled — a twelve-patient series, an eleven-patient series, two case reports, and one placebo-controlled trial that prevented post-mastectomy pain rather than treating an established one — while the enormous literature behind it is procedural anaesthesia.
quote: In a double-blinded placebo-controlled study, we enrolled 12 patients with unilateral CRPS I of the hand in the chronic state. … Pain intensity was not modulated after intervention.
corrected_wording: Its neuropathic-pain evidence is thin and almost entirely uncontrolled — a twelve-patient series, an eleven-patient series, two case reports, and one placebo-controlled trial that prevented post-mastectomy pain rather than treating an established one; placebo-controlled trials that applied the cream to the forearm rather than the painful area, to guide sensory relearning, exist in complex regional pain syndrome type I (Strauss 2015, one application, pain intensity unchanged) and in carpal tunnel syndrome (Flondell 2017 and 2024, no separate pain measure, no difference from placebo) — while the enormous literature behind it is procedural anaesthesia.
notes: Rests on Strauss 2015 (PMID 26270587), found by a PubMed search for forearm-anaesthesia trials that this paper prompted (not from its reference list); abstract cached; the cream's identity (EMLA) and the crossover design with randomised session order come from the full paper reprinted in the first author's dissertation (free, d-nb.info/113254338X/34). Flondell 2017 (this paper) and Flondell 2024 add placebo-controlled trials in carpal tunnel syndrome without a pain endpoint as such. page: Lidocaine [dose figure omitted] + prilocaine [dose figure omitted] cream (generic EMLA, ANDA), [pack size omitted], Rx (United States) — the multi-tube pack row
section: Properties › Why (opening sentence); Why For Purpose (evidence sentence)
sentence_as_it_stands: Good: Met Intended Purpose is Kinda — two small uncontrolled studies of EMLA itself in postherpetic neuralgia reported improvement, a positive result however weak, and no placebo-controlled trial in established neuropathic pain is indexed in PubMed. … [Why For Purpose] EMLA has two small uncontrolled studies of its own in postherpetic neuralgia and one placebo-controlled trial of prevention after breast surgery; no placebo-controlled trial in established neuropathic pain is indexed in PubMed, so its evidence is weak
quote: In a double-blinded placebo-controlled study, we enrolled 12 patients with unilateral CRPS I of the hand in the chronic state. … Pain intensity was not modulated after intervention.
corrected_wording: Good: Met Intended Purpose is Kinda — two small uncontrolled studies of EMLA itself in postherpetic neuralgia reported improvement, a positive result however weak, and no placebo-controlled trial of it on the painful area in established neuropathic pain is indexed in PubMed; the placebo-controlled trials in established pain states applied it to the forearm to guide sensory relearning — in complex regional pain syndrome type I, where pain did not change after one application (Strauss 2015), and in carpal tunnel syndrome, with no separate pain measure and no difference from placebo (Flondell 2017, 2024). … [Why For Purpose] EMLA has two small uncontrolled studies of its own in postherpetic neuralgia and one placebo-controlled trial of prevention after breast surgery; no placebo-controlled trial of it on the painful area in established neuropathic pain is indexed in PubMed (the placebo-controlled trials in established pain states applied it to the forearm for sensory relearning: Strauss 2015, Flondell 2017, Flondell 2024), so its evidence is weak
notes: Rests on Strauss 2015 (PMID 26270587), found by a PubMed search for forearm-anaesthesia trials that this paper prompted (not from its reference list); abstract cached; the cream's identity (EMLA) and the crossover design with randomised session order come from the full paper reprinted in the first author's dissertation (free, d-nb.info/113254338X/34). Flondell 2017 (this paper) and Flondell 2024 add placebo-controlled trials in carpal tunnel syndrome without a pain endpoint as such. Ambiguous, hence low: CRPS type I has no demonstrable nerve lesion and does not meet the IASP definition of neuropathic pain, although the record counts CRPS trials in its neuropathic-pain evidence (Reference §1.4, §4.11.6, §4.17.1) and the D067 searches included 'complex regional'; and every one of these trials put the cream on the forearm, not the painful area, so none tests the use the record evaluates and no verdict or rank change follows. Checked at the coordinator's request (pointer from the S-686-07 worker). The same two sentences appear verbatim in all three US generic rows (F05, F06, F07). On its literal reading the sentence is wrong under the record's own scope (Strauss 2015 is an indexed placebo-controlled trial in an established pain state with pain measured, and PubMed indexes Flondell 2017 as a randomised controlled trial in carpal tunnel syndrome); read as 'no placebo-controlled trial of EMLA on the painful area as treatment' it is accurate. Met Intended Purpose (Kinda) and the Decision are unaffected in my reading, since neither trial tests on-site use; the row's 'What would change this' ('Nothing short of a placebo-controlled trial in established neuropathic pain.'; in the GoodRx row 'A placebo-controlled trial of lidocaine with prilocaine in established neuropathic pain would move the fit either way') is literally met by Strauss 2015 and would read accurately as 'a placebo-controlled trial of the cream on the painful area in established neuropathic pain'. Moghtaderi 2009 (randomised, open-label, against a steroid injection) is not placebo-controlled and does not contradict this sentence.

page: EMLA anaesthetic disc (AstraZeneca) lidocaine [dose figure omitted] + prilocaine [dose figure omitted] — discontinued (United States)
sentence_as_it_stands: Its one placebo-controlled trial is prevention, not treatment: perioperative EMLA reduced chronic pain three months after breast-cancer surgery in 46 women \[Fassoulaki 2000, *Reg Anesth Pain Med*, doi:10.1053/rapm.2000.7812\].
quote: In a double-blinded placebo-controlled study, we enrolled 12 patients with unilateral CRPS I of the hand in the chronic state. … Pain intensity was not modulated after intervention.
corrected_wording: Its one placebo-controlled trial with a pain endpoint on the area at risk is prevention, not treatment: perioperative EMLA reduced chronic pain three months after breast-cancer surgery in 46 women [Fassoulaki 2000, Reg Anesth Pain Med, doi:10.1053/rapm.2000.7812]; placebo-controlled trials that applied the emulsion to the forearm to guide sensory relearning found no change in pain after one application in complex regional pain syndrome type I [Strauss 2015, Pain, doi:10.1097/j.pain.0000000000000324] and no difference from placebo in carpal tunnel syndrome, where pain was not measured separately [Flondell 2017, doi:10.1080/2000656X.2016.1205503; Flondell 2024, doi:10.1055/s-0044-1792169].
notes: Rests on Strauss 2015 (PMID 26270587), found by a PubMed search for forearm-anaesthesia trials that this paper prompted (not from its reference list); abstract cached; the cream's identity (EMLA) and the crossover design with randomised session order come from the full paper reprinted in the first author's dissertation (free, d-nb.info/113254338X/34). Flondell 2017 (this paper) and Flondell 2024 add placebo-controlled trials in carpal tunnel syndrome without a pain endpoint as such. Ambiguous, hence low: CRPS type I has no demonstrable nerve lesion and does not meet the IASP definition of neuropathic pain, although the record counts CRPS trials in its neuropathic-pain evidence (Reference §1.4, §4.11.6, §4.17.1) and the D067 searches included 'complex regional'; and every one of these trials put the cream on the forearm, not the painful area, so none tests the use the record evaluates and no verdict or rank change follows. In context the sentence counts the emulsion's placebo-controlled trials bearing on neuropathic pain; Strauss 2015 is one in an established pain state (treatment setting, single forearm application) and the carpal tunnel trials are two more without a pain endpoint as such. 'What would change this' ('To Yes: a controlled trial of the lidocaine and prilocaine emulsion as a treatment for neuropathic pain') is accurate as it stands, since none of these trials applied the emulsion to the painful area as treatment.
